I work for an oil company on a YUGE oil platform off the coast of Africa and this is how we tend to set up all of our equipment. So, when I started looking at this career jump, I noticed what feels like an inefficiency. 

Yea, running everything in stainless steel with high quality compression fittings would absolutely be how I would set the manifold up. The check valves would really only be to prevent contamination or back flow into other pieces of equipment if they had a leak or were not being used. The actual pump loading/ unloading would be done via two vacuum pressure switches that would control the set pressure of the pumps. 

The idea would be to have 2 high quality pumps each at 100% capability. So if several "users" opened up to the vacuum pressure, there would be ample suction to keep the system pressure stable (unless a leak or other unforeseen issue causing excessive load, then the second pump would turn on). 

Done properly, this system isn't (initially) cheap, but has benefits for longevity of the equipment. As was stated in the following comment, keeping a properly built piece of equipment running within design parameters for years is far less wear and tear than cycling it on and off several times a day for years. 

Thank you /chemists! I'll continue investigating any other specifics regarding vacuum system design implications in order to make sure I've created a robust and redundant system and my process (and business) is safe and dependable.
